analysis.one_liner: Lets brand-name biologic drugs delay or escape Medicare's negotiated prices when a copycat biosimilar is coming or arrives.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in the final month of the 118th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite Medicare's prescription drug price negotiation program for expensive biologic drugs. It would let a brand-name drug postpone the program's negotiated "maximum fair price" for two years instead of one when a biosimilar (a copycat biologic) is in the pipeline, make that delay automatic in many cases, and let a drug drop out of negotiated pricing for any year after a biosimilar reaches the market. If the promised biosimilar never launches, the drugmaker would owe Medicare a rebate covering most — but not all — of the difference. The changes would apply to price years beginning in 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name biologic drugmakers gain the most: up to two extra years selling at market prices before Medicare's negotiated price takes effect, automatic delays triggered by a biosimilar in development, and the right to exit negotiated pricing once a biosimilar is on the market. Biosimilar manufacturers also gain, because the bill rewards entry — the brand drug leaves the negotiated-price regime when a biosimilar launches, so the copy can compete without facing a deep government-set price benchmark. Seniors could see cheaper biosimilar versions sooner in cases where a copy is genuinely close to launch, and the rebate protects Medicare when a promised copy never materializes.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the negotiation delay from one year to two when a biosimilar maker shows a real path to market, and makes the delay automatic if the biosimilar maker has an FDA-accepted application, an ongoing clinical study, or states it expects to launch within two years.

Lets a brand biologic leave Medicare's negotiated-price regime for any year that follows a biosimilar's entry into the market, rather than only escaping negotiation before the first price year begins.
Raises the bar for the government to deny a delay, requiring 'clear and convincing evidence' that the biosimilar will actually be marketed.
Backstops Medicare with rebates — 75% of the excess price for Part D drugs and 80% for Part B drugs — if a drugmaker's promised biosimilar is never licensed and marketed by the deadline.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Every delayed negotiation is a year — or two — in which a drug sells at its market price instead of its negotiated price, showing up in seniors' copays and federal drug spending, and a portion of the negotiated discount (20–25% under the rebate formula) is never collected even when a delay fails to produce a biosimilar. Savings instead depend on biosimilars actually entering the market and undercutting the brand.

drawbacks.text: Each automatic delay pushes back the year a drug's negotiated price takes effect, so beneficiaries and the Medicare program pay higher market prices for up to two additional years on some of the program's most expensive drugs.

The automatic delay can be triggered by the biosimilar maker's own communications — including a press statement that it merely 'expects' to market the copy within two years — putting industry announcements in control of when a drug escapes negotiation.

The rebate only applies if the biosimilar is never licensed and marketed by the two-year deadline; a biosimilar that launches and then leaves the market leaves the intervening years of higher prices with no clawback.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine upside is faster biosimilar competition in cases where a copy is truly close to launch — biosimilars typically sell well below the brand, and the rebate discourages sham delays. But the price of that upside is a weaker negotiated-price guarantee: Medicare's negotiated prices were designed to lock in large, certain discounts, while this design substitutes a probable, smaller discount from biosimilar competition and gives drugmakers two extra years at market prices even when entry is real. The leverage shifts from Medicare's negotiators to drugmakers and biosimilar entrants, and the change applies to all qualifying price years starting in 2027.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate's final weeks, it was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) introduced the bill on December 9, 2024, less than a month before the 118th Congress expired.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing happened, so Medicare's drug price negotiation program stands exactly as written and beneficiaries keep the negotiated discounts current law provides; brand-name biologic makers avoided new rebates and delays but gained nothing either.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 9, 2024 and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill gives brand makers up to two extra years at unregulated prices through automatic negotiation delays, lets them exit negotiated pricing once a biosimilar launches, and raises the evidence bar the government must meet to force negotiation. Their gain comes directly at the cost of the negotiated discounts Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers would otherwise receive.

The bill rewards biosimilar entry: once a copy reaches the market, the reference drug leaves the negotiated-price regime, so biosimilar firms can launch without competing against a deeply negotiated price. Real biosimilar competition does lower costs for patients, but under this bill that benefit exists only because the government gives up part of its negotiated price.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plan sponsors and PBMs negotiate rebates against drug list prices; delayed negotiated prices keep list prices higher, raising plan costs and premiums, while any biosimilar entry would lower them. The bill leaves their role untouched either way.
